title: PSG-Nav: Probabilistic Scene Graph Navigation
one_liner: Navigate with uncertain perceptions by building a map that stores multiple possibilities for each object, then sampling multiple plausible worlds to find the best path.
lead: A robot navigating in a new building faces a big problem: its camera sometimes misidentifies objects (is that a sofa or a bed?). Existing robots throw away this uncertainty and commit to a single label, which causes navigation mistakes that compound. This paper keeps all the possibilities alive in a map, samples multiple plausible worlds from that map, and uses past successes and failures to correct confident wrong guesses.

problem.h2: Why robots get lost when objects look ambiguous
paras: A robot navigating to find an object first builds a map of the room by looking at each camera frame. For every object it sees (a table, a chair, a lamp), it labels it once and throws the label into the map. The problem: camera labels are wrong sometimes. If the camera is 40 percent sure it saw a bed and 60 percent sure it saw a sofa, the robot picks one (say, bed) and forgets about the other possibility.

When the robot later tries to navigate to the bed, it trusts this single label completely. But if the label was wrong, the robot wastes time walking to the wrong object. Worse, these misidentifications stack up across the whole map, building an incoherent layout where a bed is next to a lamp that should never coexist. The robot's navigation plan then becomes unreliable—it commits to paths based on a map riddled with unexamined errors.

callout.html: The paper keeps every possibility for each object in the map, samples multiple plausible room interpretations from these possibilities, and checks each candidate against memories of past mistakes and successes.

steps.text: For every object seen, store the full range of how likely it is to be each category (bed, table, sofa, etc.), not just the top guess.
Randomly draw 5 complete room interpretations from the distribution map. Each world picks one label per object, but different worlds pick different assignments.
For each object the robot could walk to, check: how often does it appear as a plausible landmark across the sampled worlds?
When a candidate is found, search the robot's memory for visually similar moments where the same object either succeeded or failed.
Raise confidence for candidates that match success memories, lower it for those matching failures, then execute the navigation plan.

paras: Instead of storing a single hard label (bed) for each object, the paper stores a full probability distribution (40% bed, 60% sofa, 5% couch). This distribution is updated each time the object is seen in a new frame, accumulating evidence without erasing alternative possibilities.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: Semantic consistency across plausible worlds
hidden.name: Landmark stability across sampled worlds
paras: The paper measures a quantity that doesn't show up in the camera output directly: how stable is a navigation landmark across multiple plausible room interpretations? If every sampled world agrees that the sofa is on the north wall, it is a stable landmark. If some worlds put it north and some put it west, the landmark is unstable and worth less for navigation.

The paper estimates this by Monte Carlo sampling (randomly drawing 5 complete room configurations from the distribution map) and counting how often each potential navigation goal appears in those samples. A goal that appears in 4 out of 5 worlds is far more reliable than one in 1 out of 5 because if the object keeps showing up even when the room layout changes, it means the detection is grounded in the camera data and not just a side effect of one particular label choice. A goal that vanishes when the room configuration shifts is probably a hallucination created by committing to a wrong label.

heat.caption: Darker means the sofa appears as a plausible landmark in that world. Consistent appearance means high trust.

reads.html: When a robot looks for an object, it should trust locations where the object appears in multiple different plausible room arrangements. A location that vanishes when the room layout changes is a false positive.

The 3D-PSG maintains a categorical distribution for each object node. The Multiverse Decision module samples multiple consistent semantic configurations (worlds) from these distributions and selects navigation landmarks whose spatial and semantic information gains are stable across samples.

mechanism.h2: Why keeping uncertainty and sampling worlds fixes the problem
paras: The core insight: a single wrong label in a deterministic map is invisible—the robot commits fully to it and walks in the wrong direction. But if the robot keeps the full distribution (bed 40%, sofa 60%), then samples multiple complete room interpretations from that distribution, a mistake becomes visible because it appears inconsistently across samples. Some worlds interpret the object as a bed (and put related objects nearby), others as a sofa (with different neighbors). The goals that remain stable across diverse world interpretations are the ones that deserve high confidence.

Second, the paper adds a verification step using a retrieval-augmented generator: before the robot stops at a goal, it searches its memory of past successful and failed detections. If the current candidate object looks like something the robot already succeeded with, confidence goes up. If it resembles a past failure, confidence goes down. This counteracts the camera's systematic mistakes in real-world drift (for example, if the camera trained in simulation often mistakes beds for sofas in one lighting condition, the memory calibration learns to downweight sofa detections in that situation).

stages.s: RGB-D camera frame with ambiguous object
Accumulate evidence into a categorical distribution (bed: 40%, sofa: 60%)
Sample 5 plausible room configurations from this distribution
Count how often each potential goal appears in the sampled worlds
Retrieve visually similar past successes and failures
Adjust goal confidence based on memory alignment
Navigate to the most stable, memory-verified landmark

math.words: Utility of landmark equals alpha times spatial information plus semantic information, where semantic information is the fraction of sampled worlds that contain this landmark.
symbols: Total utility score for landmark i at time t
A tuning weight (how much to favor spatial discovery over semantic consistency)
Spatial information: how much new area this landmark lets the robot explore
Semantic information: fraction of sampled worlds that place this landmark at this location

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Landmark 'sofa': appears in 4 out of 5 sampled worlds -> I_sem = 4/5 = 0.8
Landmark 'bed': appears in 1 out of 5 sampled worlds -> I_sem = 1/5 = 0.2
Bed explores only 10 square meters -> I_spa(bed) = 10
Sofa scores 15.8 vs bed's 3.2, so robot navigates toward sofa.

math.note: The equation balances two goals: exploring new space and trusting landmarks that appear consistently across plausible room configurations.

charts.title: Existing method (single hard labels)
charts.note: Once a wrong label is committed, the robot wastes steps on false goals and rarely recovers.

charts.title: PSG-Nav (distributions + sampling + memory)
charts.note: Keeping uncertainty and checking against memory prevents false commits and maintains high success across attempts.

items.b: Sampling only a few worlds misses rare but correct interpretations.
items.html: If the true room layout is in the 5 percent of plausible configurations the robot did not sample, that world never gets evaluated. The robot needs enough samples (5 is illustrative; real code uses more) to cover the distribution tail.

items.b: Memory of false positives is sparse early on.
items.html: When the robot first enters an environment, it has no past successes or failures to retrieve. The Evidential Experience Calibrator works best after many navigation episodes in the same or similar spaces.

items.b: Ambiguity in the semantic distribution stays ambiguous.
items.html: If the camera truly cannot distinguish between a sofa and a bed (they look identical in this lighting), keeping the distribution does not create information. The uncertainty is real, and the robot must learn from experience which one is actually present.

When multiple world samples agree on a landmark location, and that landmark matches successful detections in memory, the robot confidently navigates to it. When worlds disagree or memory signals a past failure, the robot deprioritizes the candidate or re-evaluates.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a toy environment (e.g., a 2D grid with 3 rooms and 8 objects) where the camera label for one object is genuinely ambiguous (50% sofa, 50% bed). Manually annotate which object is actually present in each room. Run the robot navigation twice: first with a deterministic single-label map (the baseline), and second with PSG-Nav. Measure success rate (did the robot reach the goal object within a step budget?) and false-positive stops (how many times did it incorrectly commit to the wrong object?).
demo.closing: PSG-Nav should reach the true goal at higher rates and make far fewer false stops, especially when the camera is uncertain. The deterministic baseline fails visibly; PSG-Nav recovers.
